stops.name: Ulm, the house on the Bahnhofstraße
stops.campa: Albert is born at half past eleven on a Friday morning in a rented apartment on the Bahnhofstraße, the second child expected of Hermann Einstein, an featherbed-and-electrical salesman, and his wife Pauline, born Koch. His mother, seeing the newborn's oddly angular, heavy-looking head, is at first frightened that something is wrong with him; the midwife and doctors reassure her it will round out, and it does. Within a year the family leaves Ulm for Munich, where Hermann and his brother Jakob will found an electrical engineering works. Ulm itself he barely knows; he returns to it only in memory.

stops.name: Munich, the compass in the sickbed
stops.campa: Sick in bed at four or five years old in the family's Munich apartment, Albert is given a pocket compass by his father to amuse him. He turns it in his hands and watches the needle swing back always to the same unseen north, indifferent to how he twists the case, obeying a force his eyes cannot find in the room at all. The ordinary objects of his childhood, thrown balls, blown bubbles, have always seemed to him to have direct, tangible causes; this needle answers to nothing he can see or touch, and the strangeness of it lodges in him and does not leave.
stops.quote: I can still remember — or at least believe I can remember — that this experience made a deep and lasting impression upon me. Something deeply hidden had to be behind things.

stops.name: Munich, the sacred geometry booklet and the break with the Church
stops.campa: At twelve, a poor Jewish medical student named Max Talmud (later Talmey), a Thursday dinner guest of the Einsteins for years, puts into Albert's hands a little book of Euclidean plane geometry. He works through it alone that summer, calling it ever after his holy geometry booklet, astonished that a claim like the intersection of a triangle's altitudes could be proven with such certainty from bare axioms. The same season, reading the popular science volumes Talmud also brings him, he concludes that much of the Bible's history cannot be literally true, and the devout, ardent faith of his early boyhood falls away into a fierce, private freethinking.
stops.quote: Through the reading of popular scientific books I soon reached the conviction that much in the stories of the Bible could not be true... the consequence was a positively fanatic freethinking.

stops.name: Munich, the Luitpold Gymnasium and the family's departure
stops.campa: The Einstein electrical works fails to win the contract to light Munich and the family's fortunes collapse; in the summer of 1894 Hermann, Pauline, and Albert's sister Maja move to Pavia in northern Italy to try again, leaving sixteen-year-old Albert behind in Munich to finish his schooling at the Luitpold Gymnasium, boarding with a relative. He hates the school's rote drilling and military rigidity, is warned by a teacher that his mere presence undermines the class's respect, and before the year is out a doctor's certificate of nervous exhaustion, and his own restlessness, send him after his family into Italy without a diploma.
stops.quote: It is, in fact, nothing short of a miracle that the modern methods of instruction have not yet entirely strangled the holy curiosity of inquiry.

stops.name: Zurich, the failed entrance examination
stops.campa: Two years under the required age, Albert sits the entrance examination for the Federal Polytechnic in Zurich, urged on by a family friend who believes in him. He shines in the mathematics and physics papers, outscoring the examiners' expectations, but fails outright in French, botany, and politics, and is refused admission. The principal, Albin Herzog, impressed nonetheless, advises him not to retreat to Munich but to finish his schooling properly at the cantonal school in Aarau and reapply in a year without the exam. Wounded but not broken, Albert takes the advice, and Aarau, not Zurich, becomes the gate he actually walks through.

stops.name: Aarau, the Kantonsschule and the essay on the future
stops.campa: Boarding a happy year with the family of his teacher Jost Winteler in Aarau, Albert finishes his schooling in the freer, more humane Swiss system he will praise for the rest of his life, and in January renounces his German citizenship to become, for five years, a man without a country. For a French class assignment he writes 'Mes projets d'avenir,' setting down plainly the plan of study in mathematics and physics at Zurich that he means to follow, and the ambition, already, to become a teacher of theoretical science. In September he takes his matura and passes; the road to the Polytechnic opens.
stops.quote: If I have the good fortune to pass my examinations, I would go to Zurich. I would stay there for four years to study mathematics and physics. I imagine myself becoming a teacher in those branches of natural science, choosing the theoretical part of them.
stops.quote_source: School essay, 'Mes projets d'avenir,' Aarau, 18 September 1896

stops.name: Zurich, the Polytechnic and Mileva Marić
stops.campa: Albert enters the mathematics and physics teaching diploma course at the Federal Polytechnic, one of five students in Section VI A, and the only woman among them is Mileva Marić, a Serbian from Novi Sad who has crossed half of Europe against convention to study physics. He skips lectures he finds dull, in particular Hermann Minkowski's, working instead from Kirchhoff and Helmholtz in his rented room, and it is Marcel Grossmann's careful lecture notes that carry him through the exams each spring. Between Albert and Mileva a courtship of shared physics and long, searching letters begins that will outlast the Polytechnic itself.
stops.quote: I need my Dollie for building up my little theories much more than she needs me. I feel so alone... but this loneliness [is nothing] compared with the way I felt before I knew her.

stops.name: Zurich, graduation and the wilderness of unemployment
stops.campa: Einstein graduates in August 1900 with the diploma to teach mathematics and physics, but of the four graduates in his class he alone is left without a post; he believes, and later insists, that his physics professor Heinrich Weber has quietly blackballed him among academic contacts for his independence and his skipped lectures. For nearly two years he scrapes by on tutoring jobs and short substitute-teaching posts in Winterthur and Schaffhausen, applying by postcard to laboratories across Europe and hearing nothing back, while Mileva, still working toward her own diploma, twice fails the final examination that would have made her a physicist in her own right.
stops.quote: I would have found employment long ago if Weber had not played a double game with me.

stops.name: Novi Sad, the birth of Lieserl
stops.campa: Unmarried and apart from Albert, who is job-hunting in Switzerland, Mileva returns to her parents' house in Novi Sad to bear their daughter in January 1902, a girl the letters call Lieserl. Albert, still awaiting word, writes anxiously asking after the baby's health and eyes, and says he loves her already though he has not seen her. After this single winter the child disappears from every surviving letter and record: whether she was given up for adoption, died of scarlet fever, or was cared for by Mileva's family is never afterward set down by either parent, and the mystery of Lieserl closes over itself for good.
stops.quote: Is she healthy, and does she already cry properly to make her lungs strong? What kind of eyes does she have? Which one of us does she resemble more?

stops.name: Bern, the post at the patent office
stops.campa: On his friend Marcel Grossmann's recommendation, Einstein is hired as a technical expert third class at the Federal Office for Intellectual Property in Bern, examining patent applications for electrical devices at a salary that at last lets him think of marriage. He takes a room on the corner of Speichergasse and Genfergasse, across from the clock tower whose bells will later help him picture two observers disagreeing about simultaneity. The work suits him: orderly, well-paid, undemanding enough to leave his mind free, so that within it, in the evenings and on his walks home, the shape of a whole new physics begins to gather.
stops.quote: That worldly cloister where I hatched my most beautiful ideas.
stops.quote_source: Recollection of the Bern patent office, as recorded by colleagues and biographers

stops.name: Bern, the Olympia Academy
stops.campa: In rooms he shares with his young friends Conrad Habicht and Maurice Solovine, Einstein founds, half in jest and wholly in earnest, the Akademie Olympia: three young men reading Hume, Mach, Poincaré, and Spinoza aloud over bread, cheese, and sausage late into the night, and arguing until the arguments turn to laughter. It is an academy with no professors, no doctrine, and no members but themselves, and Einstein will look back on it for the rest of his life as the true seedbed of his physics, more formative than any lecture hall he ever sat in as a student.
stops.quote: The Olympia Academy, in its glorious and dignified inactivity, still lights up our lonely lives from time to time with its cheerful eye.

stops.name: Bern, the marriage to Mileva
stops.campa: With only Habicht and Solovine as witnesses, Albert and Mileva marry in a brief civil ceremony in Bern; his mother Pauline, who considers Mileva too old and too much a physicist for her son, does not attend and does not forgive it for years. That night, the story runs, Einstein returns home from the small wedding dinner to find he has forgotten his key, and wakes his landlady rather than his bride to let him in. The household that forms in the Kramgasse apartment above a delicatessen is a working household of two physicists, Mileva keeping the accounts of a marriage that will carry the annus mirabilis within two years.
